questions.question: Explain why a circuit must be a complete path and how a break anywhere affects it, identify the components that have polarity and how their correct orientation is recognised, and state where a switch and a protective resistor are placed.
questions.expected_answer: A circuit conducts only when charge can leave one terminal of the supply, pass through the conductors and components and return to the other terminal; a break anywhere, such as a loose clip, open switch, snapped wire or blown filament, stops the whole circuit, so a non-working circuit is first traced for a complete path with firm joints, clips on metal and stripped wires. A cell has a positive terminal marked by a raised button and plus sign and a flat negative, and cells in a battery are joined positive to negative so voltages add; a light-emitting diode passes current only from its longer anode leg to its shorter cathode leg beside the flat edge of the case; a buzzer has a red positive and black negative lead; a motor runs either way and reverses when its connections are swapped, while lamps, resistors and switches have no polarity. A switch is placed in the single loop so that opening it breaks the whole circuit, and a protective resistor is placed in series with the component it protects so that all the current through that component also passes through the resistor.

questions.question: Define a short circuit, give examples, explain why it is dangerous and why a lamp bypassed by a lead goes out, and describe how fuses, circuit breakers and earth-leakage units provide protection.
questions.expected_answer: A short circuit is a very low resistance path that connects the supply terminals directly or bypasses a component, such as a bare wire across a cell, a lead across a lamp's terminals, worn wires touching or a nail through a cable. With almost nothing to resist it, the current rises to the maximum the supply can deliver, heating wires and the supply, melting insulation, draining or bursting cells and in homes igniting nearby material, making shorts the commonest cause of electrical fires. A lamp bypassed by a lead goes out because current divides between parallel paths in inverse proportion to resistance, so the near-zero path takes almost all of it and the lead warms with the energy that should have been light. A fuse is a thin wire that melts at a stated current, breaking the circuit in a fraction of a second under a short; a circuit breaker trips a switch by electromagnet or heated strip at its rated current and can be reset, with a breaker per circuit on the distribution board; an earth-leakage unit compares live and neutral currents and trips when about 30 milliamps leaks to earth through a person or damp appliance, protecting people rather than wiring.

questions.question: Describe the accepted symbols for a cell, battery, switch, push switch, lamp, resistor, LED, buzzer, motor and fuse and the conventions for wires, and state the rules for drawing a neat circuit diagram and for reading one.
questions.expected_answer: A cell is a long thin line for positive beside a short thick line for negative; a battery is several such pairs or two with a dashed line between; a switch is a line with a hinged gap; a push switch is a bar pressed onto two contacts; a lamp is a circle with a cross; a resistor is a rectangle, or a zigzag in older books, with an arrow across for a variable resistor; a light-emitting diode is a triangle with a bar at its point and two small arrows leaving, pointing in the direction of current; a buzzer is a half-circle on a base; a motor is a circle containing M; a fuse is a rectangle with a line through its length; wires are straight lines joined at a dot and crossing without a dot where unconnected. A neat diagram places components on the sides of a ruled rectangle with the supply at the top or left and positive to the left or top, uses horizontal and vertical lines with right-angle corners, standard uncrowded symbols, labels for values such as 3 V and 330 ohms, and shows the switch open. A diagram is read by finding the supply, tracing the loop, naming each component in order, checking the polarity of cells and LEDs, and looking for any line that bypasses a component, which is a short on paper.
